{{< include latex-macros/macros.qmd >}}

**Propensity score methods** are an alternative approach
to [confounding](#def-confounding-obs) adjustment in [observational studies](#sec-causal-observational).
They replace adjustment for a high-dimensional [confounder](#def-confounder) set $\vec{L}$
with adjustment for a single scalar summary:
the propensity score.

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-propensity-score}
#### Propensity score

The **propensity score** is the [conditional probability](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#def-conditional-prob) of treatment
given the observed [covariates](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-predictors):
$$e(\vec{L}) \eqdef \Pf{A = 1 \mid \vec{L}}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include _subfiles/causal-inference/_exm-propensity-score.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-propensity-score-balancing}
#### Propensity scores and exchangeability

@rosenbaum1983central showed that
if $A \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1)) \mid \vec{L}$
([conditional exchangeability](#def-exchangeability) given $\vec{L}$),
then also:
$$A \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1)) \mid e(\vec{L})$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-balancing-score}
#### Balancing score

In other words, the propensity score (@def-propensity-score) is a **balancing score**:
conditioning on the propensity score is sufficient
to remove confounding.
:::

## Propensity score estimation {#sec-ps-estimation}

The propensity score is estimated by fitting a model
for the probability of treatment given [covariates](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-predictors),
typically using [logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd#def-logistic-regression):

$$\text{logit}(\hat{e}(\vec{L}_i)) =
\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 L_{i1} + \cdots + \hat{\beta}_p L_{ip}$$

The estimated propensity score $\hat{e}(\vec{L}_i)$
is the predicted probability of treatment for each individual.

## Propensity score methods {#sec-ps-methods}

There are four main ways to use the propensity score:

1. **Matching**: Match each treated individual to one or more
   untreated individuals with similar propensity scores.
   The matched dataset is then analyzed as a simple comparison.

2. **Stratification (subclassification)**: Divide individuals
   into strata based on propensity score [quantiles](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/nonparametric-models.html#def-sample-quantile).
   Estimate the causal effect within each stratum,
   then combine across strata.

3. **Inverse probability weighting (IPW)**:
   Weight each individual by the inverse of their probability
   of receiving the treatment they actually received.
   See @def-ipw.

4. **Covariate adjustment using the propensity score**:
   Include the estimated propensity score as a [covariate](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-predictors)
   in a [regression model](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-regression-model) for the [outcome](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-outcome).

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-ipw}
#### Inverse probability weighting (IPW)

The **inverse probability weighted (IPW)** estimator
of the [ATE](#def-ate) uses weights:
$$w_i \eqdef \frac{A_i}{\hat{e}(\vec{L}_i)} +
\frac{1 - A_i}{1 - \hat{e}(\vec{L}_i)}$$

The IPW estimator of $\E{Y(a)}$ is:
$$\Est{\E{Y(a)}}_{\text{IPW}} \eqdef
\frac{\sum_{i: A_i = a} w_i Y_i}{\sum_{i: A_i = a} w_i}$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-pseudo-population}
#### Pseudo-population

Reweighting by the weights $w_i$ of @def-ipw creates a **pseudo-population**
in which treatment is [independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-indpt) of covariates,
effectively removing [confounding](#def-confounding-obs).
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include _subfiles/causal-inference/_thm-ipw-identification.qmd >}}

{{< slidebreak >}}

{{< include _subfiles/causal-inference/_exm-ipw.qmd >}}

## Propensity score example: WCGS {#sec-ps-wcgs}

In the WCGS study,
we can use propensity score methods
to estimate the causal effect of Type A behavior on CHD.
We first fit a [logistic regression](logistic-regression.qmd#def-logistic-regression) model
predicting Type A behavior from the [confounders](#def-confounder)
identified by the DAG (@sec-pred-sel-wcgs-dag):

```{r}
#| label: ps-wcgs-setup
#| code-fold: true

library(dplyr)

here::here() |>
  fs::path("Data/wcgs.rda") |>
  load()

wcgs_ps <-
  wcgs |>
  mutate(
    dibpat_A = as.integer(dibpat == "Type A"),
    chd69_yn = as.integer(chd69 == "Yes")
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(age), !is.na(dibpat), !is.na(chd69),
    !is.na(bmi), !is.na(sbp), !is.na(chol), !is.na(smoke)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: ps-wcgs-model
#| code-fold: true

ps_model <- glm(
  dibpat_A ~ age + bmi + sbp + chol + smoke,
  data = wcgs_ps,
  family = binomial()
)

wcgs_ps <- wcgs_ps |>
  mutate(
    ps = predict(ps_model, type = "response"),
    ipw = dibpat_A / ps + (1 - dibpat_A) / (1 - ps)
  )
```

::: {#fig-ps-wcgs}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(wcgs_ps, aes(x = ps, fill = factor(dibpat_A))) +
  geom_histogram(alpha = 0.6, bins = 30, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("steelblue", "tomato"),
    labels = c("Type B", "Type A"),
    name = "Personality type"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Estimated propensity score",
    y = "Count",
    title = "Propensity score distributions by personality type (WCGS)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

Distribution of estimated propensity scores
by personality type in the WCGS study.
Good overlap between the two groups
(the **overlap** or **common support** assumption)
supports [positivity](#def-positivity).

:::

::: {#tbl-ps-wcgs-ipw}

```{r}
#| label: ps-wcgs-ipw
#| code-fold: true

library(gtsummary)

outcome_ipw <- glm(
  chd69_yn ~ dibpat_A,
  data = wcgs_ps,
  weights = ipw,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

outcome_ipw |>
  tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  bold_labels()
```

Inverse probability weighted (IPW) logistic regression model for the effect of Type A personality on CHD in WCGS.

:::

::: notes

The IPW-weighted odds ratio for Type A vs. Type B behavior
estimates the causal odds ratio for CHD,
adjusting for [confounding](#def-confounding-obs) by age, BMI, SBP, cholesterol, and smoking.

Compare this to the unadjusted estimate:
the difference reflects the degree of confounding
in the WCGS data.

:::
